title: Low-latency trading, box 1: the market-data path

beats.text: Box one. How does a market data packet reach your trading strategy?
The exchange sends a packet. It lands on the network card. The operating system kernel copies it, processes it, and finally wakes up your program.
Every step costs time. Interrupts, system calls, and memory copies add up to tens of microseconds.
So why use the kernel at all? It is simple, it is safe, and it is fast enough for most firms. If your edge is measured in milliseconds, stop here.
Option two is kernel bypass. The network card writes packets straight into your program's memory. A pinned CPU core spins, and polls for new data. The kernel is out of the path.
The receive path drops to about a microsecond. The price is a dedicated core that always runs at one hundred percent, plus special network cards and software.
Option three puts the decision on an FPGA, right next to the wire. The chip parses the packet and can send an order before a CPU even sees the data. That takes hundreds of nanoseconds.
The price is engineering time. Hardware logic is slow to change, so firms keep only the simplest and fastest decisions in silicon.
So. Kernel sockets for milliseconds. Kernel bypass for microseconds. FPGA for nanoseconds. Next box: the order book.
